## Summary and general expectations of theory

The core of this theory is that front-line agents of election manipulation campaigns face real risks of exposure and punishment, even when their patron remains in office. When deciding whether and how to participate in an election-manipulation scheme, agents must weigh the risks of exposure against the risks of displeasing their political patrons.^[The risk of being cut off from the patronage network for failing to deliver sufficient votes is real. However, the risk is mitigated by the fact that principals can only imperfectly monitor their agents. It is difficult for a principal to know, for instance, how much of a positive electoral result is due to the agent's efforts and how much is due to her own local popularity. Moreover, it is difficult for the principal to know how many votes are being produced per unit of cost, and how much the agent is pocketing for himself. Incumbents have developed a variety of tools to try to circumvent this problem, like turnout-buying [@gans-morse_varieties_2014] and rewarding agents for public rallies [@szwarcberg_political_2014]. These methods are imperfect, and some---like maintaining original, correct election protocols in addition to the official, doctored versions---actually increase the risk of exposure to agents. Consequently, while the probability that electoral misdeeds will be exposed can sometimes be low, so too can the probability that defection will be discovered by the principal.] This provides the first testable implication of the theory: it implies that *some agents must face serious criminal or other personal penalties when caught cheating in elections*. This implication is tested and confirmed in [CHAPTER ON COURTS], which uses original data to show how electoral crimes and prosecuted and punished in authoritarian Russia.

Second, the agent-risk theoretical approach implies that it will be more difficult to recruit willing agents as the risk of punishment increases; illicit acts that are easily attributable to the perpetrator should decline as risk of exposure increases. As a result, *the type of manipulation observed should vary according to local conditions*. This prediction is articulated in more detail in [RUSSIA FORENSIC CHAPTER], which shows that election manipulation strategies that are more attributable (i.e. falsification) decline as local competitiveness increases. This decline is not universal; less attributable types of manipulation increase when patronage is consolidated [RUSSIA AND UKRAINE CHAPTERS]. Lastly, we should expect agents to update their estimation of local risks over time. *When an agent is harshly punished for illicit manipulation, subsequent manipulation in that region should decline.* However, by the same token, *when an exposed agent receives little to no penalty for illicit manipulation, subsequent manipulation in that region should increase.* This prediction is confirmed in [COURTS CHAPTER].

Finally, the theory makes a prediction that contravenes conventional wisdom on the relationship between protest risk and manipulation. Rather than serve as a deterrent, increasing protest risk should incentivize incumbents to devote more of their resources in manipulation efforts. Extensive electoral manipulation sends signals to elites about the resources, capacities, and intentions of the incumbent. It is a costly signal due to the principal-agent nature of manipulation, and thus serves as a credible commitment mechanism in intra-elite bargaining over spoils. The more extensively the incumbent is able to manipulate, the more elites have to lose by siding with protesters in favor of new elections. 

In other words, the theory predicts that *incubments should manipulate more when they face strong oppositions*, rather than moderate their behavior, as conventional wisdom might hold, and that when post-election protests do occur, *greater electoral manipulation will be associated with quicker defeat of protest movements.* This proposition is tested in [CROSS NATIONAL CHAPTER]. 

[CONSIDER ADDING PROTEST INSENSITIVE TO MANIPULATION AS TESTED IMPLICATION--this exists in cross-national chapter but needs to be contextualized]

## Conclusion

By shifting the analytical focus from leaders' incentives to those of front-line agents, this theory identifies new constraints on election manipulation efforts: those factors which increase the likelihood that perpetrators of illicit manipulation will be identified and punished. As such factors---like local political competition, independent courts and prosecutors, and active local media and civil society organizations---become more prominent, it is more difficult for incumbents to recruit agents to perform the most attributable forms of manipulation. Unfortunately for incumbents, these are also the techniques that tend to be most cost-effective; it is far cheaper to add five hundred votes to the ruling party's tally at the stroke of a pen, than to actually *buy* five hundred votes from the community. This helps explain how authoritarian regimes can disintegrate from the bottom-up, as opposition groups steadily gain power at the local level; it also points toward policy mechanisms that can help uphold election integrity.

However, it also suggests that protest risk will rarely deter incumbents from engaging in as much electoral manipulation as they can, as they steadily develop greater and greater social control. This is a pessimistic account for democratization in authoritarian regimes, which also highlights some possible 'red lines' for democratic erosion in established democracies. Democratic incumbents who succeed in politicizing control over patronage resources and over the legal system are building tools that may in able them to win rigged elections *and* survive the associated popular blowback.

### Variation in manipulation tactic as response to agent risk

While ballot-stuffing, voter pressure, and falsification can all add to the incumbent's tally in the election, considerable scholarship has been invested in understanding why incumbents may prefer one strategy or another. Incumbents may prefer a certain mix of strategies in order to evade observation [@asunka2017electoral] and loss of legitimacy [@vanham2015sticks], due to resource constraints [@greene_why_2007] or availability [@Frye2018], to avoid appearing weak [@Harvey2020] or to evade the strictures of modern electoral procedure [@kuo_teorell_2017]. With few exceptions [@rundlett2016deliver;@Harvey2019], front-line agents' cooperation with incumbents' preferences is often assumed.

However, front-line agents do indeed have agency, and are not indifferent among the choices on the menu of manipulation. In particular, different illegal election manipulation tactics can be traced back to their individual perpetrators with varying degrees of difficulty. This affects the degree of personal risk to which the agent is exposed. Table \@ref(tab:attribution) summarizes these differences. To be clear, it is likely not typically the case that the principal is trying to get the agent to adopt one manipulation tactic, but the agent chooses another. Instead, as conditions change, it becomes harder for principals to recruit agents to perform certain kinds of tasks (e.g. precinct officials to stuff ballot boxes), forcing them to rely on different agents who perform different tasks (e.g. party operatives to buy votes).

\textbf{Manipulation tactic} & \textbf{Perpetrators known} & \textbf{Location known} & \textbf{Time known} & \textbf{Attributability} \\ \midrule
Falsification                & Yes (Officials)                & Yes      & Yes       & High     \\
Ballot-stuffing              & Possibly (Officials or voters) & Possibly & Partially & Moderate \\
Vote-buying / voter pressure & Rarely (Various)               & No       & No        & Low      \\ \bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Variation in how attributable election manipulation tactics are to perpetrators}
\label{tab:attribution}

To my knowledge, there have been no prior studies of the factors that make electoral crimes more or less attributable to the perpetrator. However, there is a detailed literature in criminology that examines the 'solvability factors' that contribute to the likelihood of suspect arrest and case clearance in other crimes.^[While some research in this literature focuses on violent crime, the bulk of the literature focuses on solvability factors of non-violent 'volume crimes' like burglary.] An influential early study of policing in American cities concluded that "If information that uniquely identifies the perpetrator is not presented at the time the crime is reported, the perpetrator, by and large, will not be subsequently identified" [@greenwoodCriminalInvestigationProcess1975, p. ix]. This finding has been consistent in more recent research [@coupeModellingPoliceSuccess2001;@coupeDaylightDarknessTargeting2006;@olphinSolvingBurglaryOffences2021;@robinsonFactorsInfluencingPolice2009]. The effects can be large; one study finds that being caught at the scene increases the likelihood of attribution of a burgary or theft by as much as 20,000 percent (odds ratio 207.4); on the other hand, a simple description of the suspect increases the likelihood of attribution by only 40 percent [@robinsonFactorsInfluencingPolice2009].  

A comprehensive study of UK policing found that the strongest predictor of solvability is having caught the perpetrator at the scene of the crime, though this is rare; cases where the crime is known to have taken place in a narrow time window are also more easily solved [@UnderstandingAttritionProcess]. On the basis of these trends, criminal cases are sometimes divided into three categories [@eckSolvingCrimesInvestigation1983]. First, there are cases with so few 'leads' that no amount of police effort is likely to result in a suspect being apprehended. Second, there are cases with enough initial evidence that an arrest could be made with sufficient devotion of police effort and resources. Finally, there are those cases "where the suspect has been positively identified, [which] will usually result in an arrest, even with only minimal investigative effort" [@brandl1994relationshp].  

Electoral crimes can be mapped onto these features identified in criminology research. Falsification of the vote count is the electoral crime most easily attributable to its perpetrators. Only the election officials, who are typically publicly named individuals, can count, tabulate, and record the election results; the individuals responsible for any discrepancies are thus easily identifiable. Moreover, counting the votes takes place at a known location (the polling place), as does tabulation (higher level election commissions); these activities also take place at known times (after the close of polling). Election monitors, unsurprisingly, take advantage of these facts to detect attempted manipulations.The OSCE Election Monitoring Handbook, for instance, notes that observers "should select one of their assigned polling stations at which to observe the closing procedures, and then remain there for the entire vote count"; it goes on to list detailed descriptions of the kinds of activities that monitors should be alert to [@officefordemocraticinstitutionsandhumanrightsElectionObservationHandbook2010, p. 79]. 

Similar instructions are provided for monitoring tabulation. An election monitoring guidebook from the National Democratic Institute (NDI) states that "Monitors should take note of who is present inside the voting station.... Election officials are responsible for administering the voting process.... [monitors] should observe and record the conduct of election officials in order to deter fraud, to help correct inadvertent mistakes, as well as detect and record actual irregularities" [@nationaldemocraticinstituteHowDomesticOrganizations1995, p. 71]. Due to their power, and the fixed time and location of their efforts, election officials are obvious targets of attention for those who seek to monitor and expose election fraud. This makes committing fraud an exercise in considerable risk for such officials, if they are operating in a context where monitoring by NGOs, parties, or citizens is vigorous.
    

At the other end of the spectrum of attribution are techniques where the relevant violation happens away from the polling place, both in space and in time. The actors involved are diverse and often non-public, including voters' employers and managers [@Frye2018;@fryeWorkplacePoliticsHow2025], local mayors and councilors [@Nunez2018;@Mares2019], civic organizations [@hollandMachineClientelistBrokers2015], labor unions [@LarreguyCesarMontielOleaPabloQuerubin2017], partisan neighborhood brokers [@Szwarcberg2015;@Berenschot2019], and others. Ample scholarly evidence attests to the difficulty that even their patrons have in monitoring brokers' behavior [@Aspinall2014;@stokesBrokersVotersClientelism2013;@langstonWhyClientelistBrokers2023]. Observers likewise face difficulties. The NDI handbook notes that observers should devote some attention to the atmosphere immediately outside the polling place, and should note "the identities (*or descriptions*)" of the people involved in incidents of bribery or intimidation [@nationaldemocraticinstituteHowDomesticOrganizations1995, p. 74, emphasis added]. The OSCE handbook has detailed instructions on how to evaluate the pre-election and election-day period, but unsurprisingly makes no mention of how to observe vote-buying or voter intimidation away for the polling place [@officefordemocraticinstitutionsandhumanrightsElectionObservationHandbook2010], beyond an evaluation of the formal rules limiting abuse of government resources [@officefordemocraticinstitutionsandhumanrightsHanbookObservationElection2021]. The Carter Center takes a similar approach in its guidelines for observers [@thecartercenterElectionObligationsStandards].

Recognizing these difficulties, the Russian domestic election monitoring organization Golos aimed to recruit ordinary citizens in the observation of dispersed forms of manipulation. Training materials from Golos state: 

> "Elections are not just the voting day itself, but the three months of campaigning beforehand. During this period, voters may face pressure from their superiors and illegal campaigning. Officials who are prohibited from doing so may participate in it. You may also witness the illegal use of administrative and budgetary resources in the interests of one of the candidates. All this is called 'administrative resources.' Only the voters themselves can effectively respond to this blatantly illegal behavior."

Golos goes on to provide placards that citizens can print and distribute in public places, or post on walls, to inform others of their legal rights [@HowDealAdministrative2025]. The placard encourages citizens to record photographic, audio, or video evidence of violations, and provides QR-codes that link to the authorities' online complaint portals, and to Golos' crowdsourced election violation website. These documents all illustrate the challenges facing organizations that wish to monitor and deter election violations that take place away from the polling station, and---in the Golos example---the lengths the organization must go in order to try to make such techniques attributable and risky for perpetrators. It is perhaps not surprising in this context that Golos has been the subject of increasingly harsh legal repression, and was finally forced to disband in the summer of 2025 [@alexeystrelnikovRussiasElectionWatchdog2025].

Ballot-stuffing falls somewhere in between these two extremes. Illegal ballots can be cast by election officials, of course, but can also be cast by legitimate voters or by third-parties. However, ballot-stuffing can only occur where the ballot box is, and can only occur sometime between when voting starts and ends. As a result, it is much simpler for monitors attempt to observe this kind of manipulation than it is for vote-buying and voter-pressure, which are far more dispersed and involve a more diverse range of agents. 

Consequently, if agents are indeed motivated by the desire to avoid personal attribution of electoral misdeeds, it is to be expected that agents will be less interested in techniques higher on the ladder the more likely they are to be exposed. That is, holding other factors equal, in local areas where political opposition and activist civil society are limited, we should expect to see more falsification by election officials. As the risk of exposure increases due to greater opposition and/or civil society activity, manipulation should move down the ladder in Table \@ref(tab:attribution). Election officials should shift from falsification to ballot-stuffing, and then increasingly drop out of the manipulation enterprise in favor of less easily identifiable individuals. As the risk of exposure increases further, even these third-party individuals should be less willing to manipulate in and around the polling place; instead, the incumbent will need to rely on a broader network of agents distributed throughout society. As this dispersion increases, a given 'unit' of manipulation becomes more expensive for the incumbent, as principal-agent problems mount and monitoring agents becomes more difficult.

This insight---that election-manipulating agents constrain their principals' options---produces a unique test of the regime-strength model of manipulation. Traditionally, explanations of variation in type of electoral manipulation has emphasized political leaders and their fear of legitimacy loss [@birch2011;@Schedler2013], their ability to monitor voters' compliance [@cox1981turnout;@stokes2005], their confidence in victory [@Hauser2018] or their access to certain resources [@vanham2015sticks]. Writing in 2013, Simpser noted that "the question of why some tactics of electoral manipulation are chosen over others in particular circumstances remains an open one," but sketched an expectation that incumbents would choose more cost-effective tactics over less cost-effective ones [-@simpser2013, pp. 28-29]. 

These theories suggest distinct predictions at the national and local levels. On the one hand, in a close election, theories that hinge on legitimacy costs suggest that incumbents should prioritize fraud in less-competitive regions. This is because fraud is the most cost-effective election-day manipulation strategy, but it requires control of the local election administration in order to implement. In more competitive regions, such models would seem to predict a decline in manipulation across all strategies. The difficulty in controlling the election administration in contested regions makes fraud difficult, while vote-buying, voter pressure, and voter intimidation are all more visible strategies; being directly visible to voters, their potential legitimacy cost is high if such efforts are widespread [@Schedler2013;@birch2011]. A principal-focused theory of manipulation that emphasizes legitimacy costs should thus predict that all types of election-day manipulation will decrease with the risk of exposure, and that fraud should predominate where the risk of exposure is low.

Different predictions emerge if, instead, the cost-effectiveness of a given strategy for incumbents is in large party conditioned by *agents'* incentive structures (rather than by legitimacy costs to principals). We should expect to see fraud decrease with local risk of exposure, as in the principal-focused approach. However, we should expect to see *less attributable*, though still visible forms of manipulation, *increase* with local risk of exposure. This outcome is expected because incumbents are not deterred from manipulating by legitimacy costs; indeed, they seek to demonstrate their power and impunity through the use of manipulation [@simpser2013]. However, as local risks of exposure increase, it becomes increasingly difficult to pressure election officials into engaging in attributable falsification. Instead, incumbents must rely on less attributable techniques like vote-buying and voter-pressure, despite their significantly greater cost and lower reliability.

<!-- [Think about using the terms principal-risk vs. agent-risk models of manipulation? Possibly in addition to 'regime strength model of manipulation and protest'] -->

Theories of manipulation that focus solely on principals' incentives should generally favor increased election fraud. As electoral outcomes become more uncertain, both the likelihood of losing office and the likelihood of significant post-election backlash increase. Incumbents are thus in a position of needing to significantly boost their vote-count while minimizing the visibility of manipulation. Falsification (and to a lesser extent ballot-stuffing) meets these criteria most effectively. It is very cost effective, requiring only that the incumbent have influence over members of the electoral administration and that they mis-report the results of the election. It does not require large networks of agents, is easily monitored (e.g. by setting vote-share and turnout targets), and can be kept hidden from voters.
